analysis.one_liner: Requires cable and satellite TV providers to rebate customers for blackout periods during channel disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would give TV subscribers rebates when carriage disputes blackout their channels, has not advanced since it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on January 30, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a TV channel goes dark because the cable or satellite company and the channel's owner are fighting over fees, subscribers keep paying for a package that is missing channels. This bill would order the Federal Communications Commission to write rules requiring those providers to automatically refund subscribers for the period a promised channel is blacked out. The bill has been referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable and satellite TV subscribers, especially sports fans, who lose access to a channel they paid for during a carriage dispute. When a broadcaster and a distributor fail to agree on fees and the channel goes dark, customers would get money back for the days the channel was off the air, rather than paying full price for a partial service.

how_it_helps.text: Requires cable and satellite providers to issue a rebate to any subscriber denied access to video programming the provider had agreed to carry, when the blackout results from a retransmission consent or carriage negotiation.
Directs the FCC to write the rules within 90 days of enactment, including determining the appropriate rebate amount.

analysis.who_pays: Cable and satellite TV providers, who would owe rebates during blackouts, and to a lesser degree broadcast station owners and programmers, whose main source of leverage in fee negotiations — threatening a blackout — becomes less one-sided once customers are compensated for outages.

drawbacks.text: A rebate only refunds part of a monthly bill; it does not restore the missing channel, so a fan can still miss games, and the FCC would have to settle on a rebate formula that may not match what a subscriber actually values.

Most carriage disputes are resolved in days, so in the typical case the rebate would be small; the bill's main effect is to change negotiating leverage rather than to deliver large direct savings to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to any one subscriber is modest — a partial refund during a blackout that usually lasts only days — but the bill is cheap to comply with and addresses a real annoyance: paying full price while a promised channel is dark. The larger effect is on bargaining dynamics, where it shifts a bit of leverage from channel owners and distributors toward customers. The costs are limited and borne by the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote since late January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the bill on January 30, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action has been taken on the bill since the referral, and it has no cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no action taken, cable, satellite, and broadcast interests keep the status quo, in which blackouts cost them nothing while they negotiate. Consumers keep paying full bills during outages.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TV distributors and broadcasters, so far

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on January 30, 2025

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, so no partisan divide has formed; it has simply not moved.

industries.note: Providers would owe automatic rebates whenever a carriage dispute blacks out a channel customers paid for. Today a blackout costs them nothing directly; the bill makes outages a refund obligation.

Programmers use the threat of pulling their channels to extract higher fees from distributors. Mandatory customer rebates during blackouts dilute that leverage, making it somewhat less profitable to keep channels dark as a bargaining tactic.
The bill applies only to cable and satellite providers, not streaming platforms, giving streaming a relative edge as consumers weigh alternatives when cable prices stay full during outages.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action more than a year into the session, the bill is unlikely to advance unless a carriage dispute generates major public attention or other senators join; most bills at this stage die in committee.
